articles.title: Barbara Kingsolver: ‘What does love feel like? At 16, breaking the speed limit. Years later, a warm bath’
articles.summary: The author on the FBI tapping her phone, teaching herself to read aged three, and why she knits in meetings. Born in Maryland, in the US, Barbara Kingsolver, 71, won a music scholarship to DePauw University in Indiana. She became a journalist and published her first novel, The Bean Trees, in 1988.
body: When were you happiest? Right after the births of my children. Those hormones are strong medicine: they erase all memory of recent gruelling events and crown you goddess, author of divine creation.
What is your greatest fear? Being on a transatlantic flight without a good book.

What is your earliest memory? Teaching myself to read, at age three. I was so covetous of whatever my father was getting from his newspaper, I picked it up after he set it aside and stared with fierce intention, naming and sounding out letters until the first whole word broke into my brain. It was “orange”.

What is the trait you most deplore in others? Refusing to take responsibility. I can forgive anything, if the offender will just say, “I did that. It was wrong, and I’m sorry.” I can’t understand why some people fight it so hard. Especially those of the male persuasion.

articles.title: ‘Seduced by a dramatic landscape of canyons and lakes’: exploring Catalonia’s wild side
articles.summary: A historic single-track train line through the foothills of the Pyrenees opens up a pristine wilderness of forests, gorges and thundering rivers. Alighting at the train station of Santa Linya in northern Spain, I paused to wonder what the railway engineers were thinking.
body: My husband and I had first strayed into this western corner of Catalonia – Pallars Jussà – on our honeymoon road trip 21 years earlier. Seduced by its dramatic landscape of canyons, lakes, crumbling ruins and the formidable Noguera Pallaresa river thundering south from the Pyrenees, we had vowed to return one day. He loves mountains, I love water, we both love abandoned buildings; it was a geographical match made in heaven. Now those vows had come good – we were back, on a mission to go deeper into the hinterland.

The menus are not the only reminder that you are very much in Catalonia. You won’t find any tapas round here; you certainly won’t find a menu in Spanish, and attempts to speak español are tolerated only from foreign visitors. In the towns, the population is small but the resistance is strong; the Estelada, the separatist flag, hangs from balconies and windows, while its red and yellow stripes are painted on roads, bridges and walls, along with pro‑independence graffiti ranging from the galvanising Fem República! (Let’s build the Republic!) to the more direct Puta España (Google it).

articles.title: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
articles.summary: One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight.
body: What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.”

He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks.

In one of the early hearings, he also receives some words of support from a court security guard, “just some normal geezer, patting me down for weapons or sharps”, who whispers: “All right, Russell. The whole country’s behind you, mate. The whole country’s behind you.”

articles.title: Inside 'Grand Theft Auto VI'—and the Real-Life Florida Locations That Inspired It
articles.summary: Gamers are leaving their consoles behind in favor of real-world trips to the locations that inspired their favourite levels. Next on the agenda? The Florida cities, towns, and national parks behind the upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6
body: Set to be released on November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of media ever created. Pre-sale estimates suggest the game has made a staggering $476 million in revenue already.

Dreamt up by Scottish developers Rockstar Games, the GTA series has been big business for some time now. The previous instalment, Grand Theft Auto V has reportedly made a whopping $11 billion since its release in 2013. Not bad for a game in which you essentially steal cars and shoot guns.

If you haven’t played the games, you should know that they take place in a sort of shadow version of the US, with each game taking place in a new city inspired by a real-world counterpart. For me, they’ve been a fascinating companion to my travels in America. When I’m in New York, walking among towering skyscrapers, I can’t help but be reminded of Liberty City, the location of 2001’s dark and atmospheric Grand Theft Auto III. On holiday in Los Angeles, driving along the Pacific Coast Highway, the long, ocean-view roads of GTA V ’s Los Santos were front of mind.
points: Gamers are leaving their consoles behind in favor of real-world trips to the locations that inspired their favourite levels.

articles.title: Inside the Y2K Costumes and Sets of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson’s ‘Mouse’
articles.summary: From vintage prom dresses to Seventeen-covered bedrooms, the designers of “Mouse” reveal how fashion and interiors bring 2002 Arkansas to life.
body: The making of Mouse gave some Arkansas mothers a very good reason to have kept their daughters’ prom dresses. Costume designer Meg Grace put out a call on Facebook; in the week before the school-dance sequence was filmed, a member of her team drove around town collecting gowns, filling a van. Altogether, they gathered some 50 dresses worn to proms between 2000 and 2003. “It felt like a time warp,” Grace says of seeing them on the actors.

That flicker of recognition runs through the funny, affecting film from Ghostlight directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Set in 2002 in O’Sullivan’s hometown of North Little Rock, Arkansas, Mouse follows Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer), a teenager accustomed to living in the shadow of her charismatic best friend, Callie (Chloe Coleman). After Callie’s sudden death, Minnie gravitates toward her friend’s poised mother, Helen ( Sophie Okonedo ), and the inviting home she has long preferred to her own. Their bond grows more complicated, shaped by affection, grief, and that familiar teenage longing to be someone else.

articles.title: How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports
articles.summary: Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop. On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States.
body: There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

articles.title: I Want What Adorable New Moms Beanie Feldstein and Bonnie-Chance Roberts Have
articles.summary: “Getting to be a mom alongside my wife is the greatest gift. She’s such a good mom, and it’s so special to watch,” Feldstein said in a recent interview.
body: Love is a many-splendored thing, especially when you’re gawking at it from the outside. In this column, we’ll be examining the celebrity couples who give us hope for our own romantic futures as we try to learn what we can from their well-documented bonds.

There was a period during what I like to call my “lesbian femcel era” (shortly after a breakup with the first woman I ever had real feelings for) when I had to mute any and all happy and in-love sapphic couples on social media in order to protect my own mental health. First up on my list? Beanie Feldstein and her wife Bonnie-Chance Roberts.

Luckily, I’m no longer down quite as bad as I used to be, which means I can enjoy Feldstein-Roberts updates—from their Gucci-clad 2023 wedding to the recent news that they’d welcomed their first child together —without undue jealousy.

articles.title: What Makes a Man of the Year? Inside GQ’s Big Night Out at the Chateau Marmont
articles.summary: GQ’s annual Men of the Year Party returned to Los Angeles, the first celebration under global editorial director Adam Baidawi, who was joined by co-hosts Chris Rock, Andrew Garfield, and Matt Damon; Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve; and Designer of the Year Michael Rider.
body: I pulled up to Chateau Marmont at 10 p.m. sharp, where hordes of photographers had congregated outside. Flashes were going off in rapid succession as I slipped out of my Uber in a pair of Marc Jacobs bow heels from the early 2010s with a giant smile on my face when not a single camera turned my way. I guess they don’t know good footwear when they see it.

I was there to cover GQ’s Men of the Year party—not to be confused with People’s Sexiest Man Alive, although I imagine there is some overlap in the tip sheets. This year, GQ was honoring not one man but five: Chris Rock, Andrew Garfield, Matt Damon, Celine’s Michael Rider, and legendary director Denis Villeneuve. Combine that with the guest list—Jason Bateman, Joshua Jackson, Travis Scott, Patrick Schwarzenegger, Miguel, Diplo, and Jordan Firstman to name a few—and it was quite the gathering of testosterone under one roof.

articles.title: Half Cruise, Half Cargo Ship? What It's Like to Sail French Polynesia Aboard a Local Freighter
articles.summary: Writer Scott Laird hops aboard a 12-night sailing with Aranui Cruises, a locally owned line that offers passenger and cargo services from Tahiti to the Marquesas Islands.
body: It’s certainly a romantic notion to hop a freighter and sail to the distant South Pacific. One could spend days at sea staring at nothing but seabirds and cargo pallets, waking up to the sound of those pallets being offloaded onto a tiny concrete wharf, meeting a community nestled among palms. One could take the day to hike or tour the island, or feast on fresh catches with the locals, while the offloaded pallets are filled with grapefruits, dried coconut husks, and flowers to be sold elsewhere— Tahiti, perhaps.

It might come as a surprise to know that one company has been offering dedicated cruises built around that very premise for over 40 years. In French Polynesia, the locally owned cruise line Aranui Cruises offers combination passenger and cargo services from Papeete, Tahiti, to the dramatically jagged volcanic pitons and pastoral scenes of the Marquesas Islands.
Fatu Hiva in the Marquesas Islands has no airport and is only accessible by sea.
